intro: Edward Neeman plays the Black Keys étude: the right hand races over the five black notes while the left supplies crisp chords and surprises in the bass. Even the final octave dash stays on the black keys.

sections.label: A · Black-note triplets, crisp left-hand chords
sections.mNote: The right hand runs; the left answers with detached chords

sections.label: B · D♭ major and left-hand calls
sections.mNote: The triplets continue while the left hand changes the harmony

sections.label: A′ · G♭ major brings back the opening
sections.mNote: The opening figure returns, then dwindles to pianissimo

sections.label: Coda · Both hands on black keys
sections.mNote: Wide arpeggios lead to a final dash in octaves

cues.title: Five black notes
cues.text: The right hand runs in semiquaver triplets over the piano’s five black notes. Below it, the left hand plays detached chords and octaves. The opening phrase is full of quick changes between forte and piano — a bold statement, then a quiet answer.
cues.evidence: Opening triplets, left-hand articulation and four-bar dynamic pattern: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._10,_No._5_(Chopin), citing Hugo Leichtentritt, Analyse der Chopin’schen Klavierwerke, vol. 2 (1922), pp. 105–106.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chopin for free
cues.text: Neeman joins the pianists recording Chopin for Musopen’s Set Chopin Free project. Launched through crowdfunding in 2013, the project seeks new recordings that anyone can download, share and use.
cues.evidence: Culture.pl, ‘Set Chopin Free’, 11 September 2013, names Edward Neeman among the project’s pianists and describes its crowdfunding and free-access purpose. https://culture.pl/en/article/set-chopin-free

cues.title: Both hands join the dash
cues.text: The coda brings the middle section’s figure back in G♭ major. Wide arpeggios spread across the keyboard, then both hands race in detached octaves on the black keys. The closing direction is fortissimo.
cues.evidence: Coda and final black-key octaves: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._10,_No._5_(Chopin), citing Leichtentritt, vol. 2, p. 109.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The triplets continue into D♭ major
transitions.from: A · Black-note triplets, crisp left-hand chords
transitions.to: B · D♭ major and left-hand calls
transitions.how: The opening moves from G♭ major to its dominant, D♭ major. The right-hand triplets keep running as the left hand changes the bass and chord pattern. The middle section stretches the opening’s neat four-bar phrases into less regular lengths.
transitions.evidence: D♭-major middle section and phrase lengths: Leichtentritt, vol. 2, pp. 106–108, summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._10,_No._5_(Chopin).

transitions.title: The left hand brings G♭ home
transitions.from: B · D♭ major and left-hand calls
transitions.to: A′ · G♭ major brings back the opening
transitions.how: The left hand’s short calls lead back to G♭ major and the opening figure. The right hand continues its black-note triplets, while the bass restores the original harmony. The return soon softens towards delicatissimo, pianissimo, smorzando — very delicate, very quiet, dying away.
transitions.evidence: Return at bar 49 and subsequent markings: Leichtentritt, vol. 2, pp. 108–109, summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._10,_No._5_(Chopin).

transitions.title: The coda spreads across the keyboard
transitions.from: A′ · G♭ major brings back the opening
transitions.to: Coda · Both hands on black keys
transitions.how: A quiet cadence leads to the coda in G♭ major. The middle section’s figure returns in the home key, then the hands spread into wide arpeggios above an ascending bass. Both hands finish with black-key octaves, marked fortissimo and detached.
transitions.evidence: Coda, rising bass and final octaves: Leichtentritt, vol. 2, p. 109, summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._10,_No._5_(Chopin).

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
